title: Following
coreIdea: Stay with one moving subject for a short period and photograph the evolving relationship between the person and their environment.
whyItMatters: It teaches sustained observation and the ability to build a small narrative through changing positions rather than isolated hits. It also forces you to manage distance, presence, and ethics in real time.
shootingBrief: Choose one subject moving through public space. Follow discreetly 5–12 minutes. Minimum coherent set of 6–8 frames. Stop if discomfort appears. Volume 40–60.
technicalFocus: Settings: AF-C, f/4–5.6, shutter 1/250s or faster.
Stance: Parallel or slightly behind, never aggressive. Keep body language neutral.
Distance: 4–10 meters. Longer end of the zoom helps.
failureModes: Producing only similar frames from the same angle.

goodVsExcellent.good: A series of the same person in different places.
goodVsExcellent.excellent: The series shows genuine change in relationship between person and place; strongest frame stands alone.

title: Behind
coreIdea: Photograph people primarily from behind or strong three-quarter rear so posture, clothing, gesture, and context carry the picture.
whyItMatters: Removes reliance on facial expression. Forces attention to body language and environment — skills that improve all street work including portraits.
shootingBrief: Only rear or strong three-quarter rear angles. Minimum 8 frames where absence of face is a strength. Volume 40–70. Dignity required.
technicalFocus: Settings: f/4–5.6, shutter fast enough for gesture.
Focusing: On upper body or strongest graphic element.
Light: Backlight and side light for separation and silhouette.
Distance: 2–6 meters. Candid. Never mock or diminish.
failureModes: Making the person look small or exploited.

goodVsExcellent.good: No full face and the picture is still readable.
goodVsExcellent.excellent: Posture, clothing, and environment create a complete character. Absence of face is a deliberate strength.

title: Looking Down
coreIdea: Change viewpoint completely. Work the ground plane — feet, shadows, discarded objects, patterns, reflections in pavement.
whyItMatters: Default eye-level is a habit, not a law. Looking down forces new subject matter and breaks compositional autopilot.
shootingBrief: Entire session looking downward. Minimum 8 intentional frames. Volume 40–60. Include tight details and wider overhead when possible.
technicalFocus: Settings: Higher shutter (1/320s+) to freeze hand movement while looking down.
Focusing: Single-point or zone on the ground plane.
Stance: Control your own shadow rigorously.
Light: Hard light creates the best ground graphics.
failureModes: Including your own feet or shadow by accident.

goodVsExcellent.good: Something interesting on the ground is recorded.
goodVsExcellent.excellent: The downward view creates a complete, self-contained world that feels intentional.

title: Blurred
coreIdea: Use intentional motion blur (panning or static camera with moving subjects) as the primary quality of the picture.
whyItMatters: Sharpness is a default, not a requirement. Controlled blur can carry energy and atmosphere that sharp frames cannot.
shootingBrief: Shutter speeds roughly 1/15s to 1/4s. Two methods: panning with a moving subject, or static camera with moving people/traffic. Minimum 6 intentional blur frames. Volume 40–70.
technicalFocus: Settings: Shutter priority or manual. Start around 1/15s. Raise ISO if needed for usable aperture.
Focusing: Pre-focus on subject plane or continuous.
Stance: Brace for static blur; smooth hip movement for panning.
failureModes: Blur that looks like a mistake.
No clear subject readable inside the blur.

goodVsExcellent.excellent: Blur has clear direction and energy; a subject still reads inside it.

title: Layers
coreIdea: Build frames with clear foreground, midground, and background that interact without collapsing into clutter.
whyItMatters: Depth and controlled complexity separate competent street pictures from flat ones. Layers also improve street portraits by placing a person in a meaningful environment.
shootingBrief: Actively seek three-plane compositions. Minimum 6 frames with clear, readable layers. Volume 40–70. Test both wider and longer ends of the lens.
technicalFocus: Settings: f/8–11 preferred for multi-plane sharpness on APS-C.
Focusing: Usually on midground or strongest subject plane.
Stance: Move your feet to control overlaps and avoid merges.
Light: Side light or backlight helps separate planes.
failureModes: Uncontrolled merges that flatten the image.
Too many planes with no hierarchy.

goodVsExcellent.excellent: Planes interact through gesture, gaze, or light and the picture remains clear rather than busy.
